## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical experience with image provenance, SBOMs, and policy enforcement in GPU-enabled Kubernetes at scale.

## Key Concepts
- Cosign signing with repository public key
- SBOM generation and verification (e.g., SPDX/SBOM formats)
- Central provenance record and digest alignment
- Kyverno or OPA gate policies for admission control
- CI integration (GitHub Actions) and runtime validation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow sketch
name: Sign and Verify Image
on: [push]
jobs:
  sign-verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: |
          docker build -t registry.example.com/project/model:tag .
      - name: Sign image
        run: |
          cosign sign --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/project/model:tag
      - name: Verify image
        run: cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/project/model:tag
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle rotation of the cosign public key in a live environment?
- What performance impact would SBOM generation introduce in CI and how to mitigate it?

name: Prove Provenance
on: [push]
jobs:

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests policy design, RBAC scoping, and CI integration for a high-sensitivity platform.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- RBAC bindings (RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding)
- Namespace-scoped allowlists and auditing in CI

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (RBACWhitelist)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: rbacwhitelist
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names: {}
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package rbacwhitelist
      violation[{msg}] {
        binding := input.review.object
        binding.kind == \"RoleBinding\" or binding.kind == \"ClusterRoleBinding\"
        role := binding.roleRef.name
        ns := binding.metadata.namespace
        allowed := data.allowlist[ns]
        role != \"\"; role notin allowed
        msg := sprintf(\"RBAC violation: %s bound to %s in %s\", [binding.kind, role, ns])
      }
```

```yaml
# Constraint (per-namespace allowlist)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: RbacWhitelist
metadata:
  name: rbac-whitelist-prod
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [\"rbac.authorization.k8s.io\"]
      kinds: [\"RoleBinding\", \"ClusterRoleBinding\"]
  parameters:
    namespaceAllowlists:
      production: [\"view\", \"edit\"]
      staging: [\"view\"]
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test this with CI/CD and simulate violations?
- How would you handle dynamic/temporary permissions without conflicting with the allowlist?

## Why This Is Asked
- Tests understanding of namespace-scoped network policies and the allow-by-default model.
- Checks ability to craft precise egress rules and test scenarios.
- Evaluates how to verify traffic patterns in a live cluster.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes NetworkPolicy basics, podSelector, egress rules
- Protocols: TCP/UDP, DNS traffic behavior
- Verification: controlled test pods and curl/dig tests

## Code Example
```yaml
# Deny-all egress by default is achieved by allowing only specific egress in a policy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-web-egress
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector: {}
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.25/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this policy for egress to a specific set of namespaces or external CIDRs?
- How would you validate that the policy is enforced in a multi-tenant environment?

## Why This Is Asked
This checks IaC policy thinking and beginner-friendly gate design for real-world Terraform repos.

## Key Concepts
- Terraform plan JSON, OPA/rego, policy-as-code, resource-type checks (snowflake_share, aws_s3_bucket).
- Handling create actions and how to surface violations in CI.

## Code Example
```rego
package terraform.enforcement

default allow = false

violation[{"msg": m}] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "snowflake_share"
  rc.change.actions contains "create"
  not rc.change.after.tags.approved == true
  m := "Snowflake share must have tags.approved=true"
}

violation[{"msg": m}] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  rc.change.actions contains "create"
  (not rc.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration) or (rc.change.after.public_access_block != true)
  m := "S3 bucket must enable encryption and block public access"
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for existing resources?
- How to extend to other providers/resources and monitor drift?

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci-manifest-gate.yml
name: Manifest Gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Validate manifests
        run: |
          set -e
          violations=0
          for f in $(git diff --name-only origin/main | grep -E '\\.ya?ml$' ); do
            if ! yq e '.spec.template.spec.containers[].readinessProbe' "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1; then violations=$((violations+1)); fi
            if ! yq e '.spec.template.spec.containers[].livenessProbe' "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1; then violations=$((violations+1)); fi
            if ! yq e '.spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot' "$f" | grep -q true; then violations=$((violations+1)); fi
            if ! yq e '.spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser' "$f" | grep -q '1000'; then violations=$((violations+1)); fi
            if ! yq e '.spec.template.spec.containers[].imagePullPolicy' "$f" | grep -q 'Always'; then violations=$((violations+1)); fi
          done
          if [ "$violations" -gt 0 ]; then exit 1; fi
```

## Why This Is Asked

This evaluates the ability to translate security requirements into automated validation for Helm-rendered Kubernetes manifests, demonstrating practical DevOps security implementation skills.

## Key Concepts

- Helm template rendering for manifest generation
- Kubernetes container securityContext enforcement
- GitHub Actions as CI/CD security gates
- Lightweight YAML validation using shell scripting

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Helm Security Gate
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'charts/**'
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-helm@v3
      - name: Render and validate security context
        run: |
          helm template myapp charts/myapp > rendered.yaml
          # Validate security context fields
          python3 scripts/validate-security.py rendered.yaml
```

```python
# scripts/validate-security.py
import sys, yaml
with open(sys.argv[1]) as f:
    docs = yaml.safe_load_all(f)
for doc in docs:
    if doc.get('kind') == 'Deployment':
        for container in doc['spec']['template']['spec']['containers']:
            ctx = container.get('securityContext', {})
            if not ctx.get('runAsNonRoot'):
                print(f"FAIL: {container['name']} missing runAsNonRoot")
                sys.exit(1)
            if not ctx.get('runAsUser', 0) >= 1000:
                print(f"FAIL: {container['name']} runAsUser < 1000")
                sys.exit(1)
            if not ctx.get('readOnlyRootFilesystem'):
                print(f"FAIL: {container['name']} missing readOnlyRootFilesystem")
                sys.exit(1)
print("All security context checks passed")
```

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:

          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          # readOnlyRootFilesystem: true  # Missing - will fail CI

          runAsUser: 1000

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests the ability to enforce Kubernetes scheduling best practices through automated CI gates. It demonstrates understanding of pod distribution for high availability, GitOps workflows, and infrastructure-as-code validation.

## Key Concepts

- **Kubernetes topologySpreadConstraints**: Controls how pods are distributed across failure domains (zones, nodes, etc.)
- **Deployment replicas and scaling**: Understanding when and why to distribute workloads
- **YAML parsing in CI pipelines**: Using Python or Node.js to validate manifests
- **GitHub Actions workflow configuration**: Building automated gates for GitOps
- **Local validation and pre-commit hooks**: Catching issues before code reaches CI

## Code Example

```python
# gate-topology.py
import sys
import yaml
import glob

def check_deploymentConstraints(doc):
    if doc.get('kind') != 'Deployment':
        return True
    
    replicas = doc.get('spec', {}).get('replicas', 1)
    if replicas <= 2:
        return True
    
    topology = doc.get('spec', {}).get('template', {}).get('spec', {})
    if 'topologySpreadConstraints' not in topology:
        return False
    
    for constraint in topology['topologySpreadConstraints']:
        if constraint.get('topologyKey') != 'topology.kubernetes.io/zone':
            return False
        maxSkew = constraint.get('maxSkew', 1)
        if maxSkew > 1:
            return False
    
    return True

def main():
    failed = []
    for manifest in glob.glob('**/*.yaml', recursive=True):
        with open(manifest) as f:
            docs = yaml.safe_load_all(f)
            for doc in docs:
                if doc and not check_deploymentConstraints(doc):
                    failed.append(manifest)
    
    if failed:
        print(f"Failing manifests: {failed}")
        sys.exit(1)
    
    print("All Deployments pass topology constraints check")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

## GitHub Actions Workflow

```yaml
name: Topology Constraints Gate
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  enforce-topology:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install pyyaml
      - name: Run topology gate
        run: python gate-topology.py
```

## Failing Manifest Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:latest
```

## Passing Manifest Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: web
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:latest
```

## How to Verify

**Local Verification:**
```bash
pip install pyyaml
python gate-topology.py
```

**CI Verification:**
The GitHub Actions workflow runs automatically on pull requests. Merges are blocked until all Deployments with replicas > 2 include proper topologySpreadConstraints.

**Pre-commit Hook:**
Add to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: topology-gate
        name: Enforce topologySpreadConstraints
        entry: python gate-topology.py
        language: system
        types: [yaml]
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of Gatekeeper policy design, basic Rego, and CI validation.

## Key Concepts
- OPA Gatekeeper, ConstraintTemplate, Constraint, Rego basics
- Pod security: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, image allowlists
- CI integration and local validation strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (conceptual)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8spodsecurity
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8SPodSecurity
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8spodsecurity
      # policy consolidated in real template
```
```yaml
# Constraint (conceptual)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8SPodSecurity
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        kinds: ["Deployment"]
  parameters:
    allowList:
      - registry.example.com/*
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle per-environment allowlists?
- How would you audit Gatekeeper decisions historically?
